title: Python
summary: The most beginner-friendly language, used for automation, data and AI. Runs here with Pyodide.

lessons.title: Python: syntax basics

concept.text:
Python reads almost like English, which makes it a popular first language. It is used for scripts, websites, data analysis and nearly all AI work.

Python uses **indentation** (spaces at the start of a line) to show which lines belong together. There are no curly braces, so tidy spacing is not optional: it is the syntax.
concept.analogy: Indentation in Python works like an outline. Sub-points are indented under their heading, and that is how everyone knows what belongs to what.

visual.caption: The same idea in Python and JavaScript.

steps.title: Variables and printing
steps.text: No keyword is needed to create a variable. f-strings insert values into text.

steps.title: Decisions
steps.text: A colon starts a block and the indented lines are inside it.

steps.title: Loops

interactive.starter:
name = "Ava"
score = 7
score += 5
print(f"{name} has {score} points")

if score >= 10:
    print("Level up!")

for n in range(1, 4):
    print(n, "squared is", n ** 2)

challenge.prompt: Print a countdown from 5 to 1, then print `Liftoff!`.
challenge.hint: `range(5, 0, -1)` counts down: start at 5, stop before 0, step by -1.

takeaways: Indentation defines blocks in Python. Use 4 spaces.
print() shows output and f-strings build text from values.
for loops iterate over lists, strings and range().

lessons.title: Python: functions, lists and dictionaries

concept.text:
Three tools carry most Python programs. A function packages reusable logic with `def`. A **list** holds ordered items. A **dictionary** maps keys to values, like a real dictionary maps words to definitions.

List comprehensions build a new list from an old one in a single readable line.
concept.analogy: A list is a numbered queue: you find people by position. A dictionary is a coat check: you hand over a ticket (the key) and get back exactly your coat (the value).

items.title: dict  {'a': 1}
items.text: Key to value lookup. Access with d['a'].

items.title: tuple  (1, 2)
items.text: Ordered, cannot change. Good for fixed pairs.

steps.title: Define a function
Use a dictionary
Comprehensions
steps.text: Read it as: give me n squared, for each n in nums, if n is even.
steps.code: squares = [n ** 2 for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]

challenge.prompt: Write `word_count(text)` that returns a dictionary counting how often each word appears, ignoring case. Test it on the sentence provided.
challenge.hint: `text.lower().split()` gives a list of words. `counts.get(word, 0) + 1` handles a word you have not seen yet.

takeaways: def creates functions. return sends a value back to the caller.
Lists are ordered sequences. Dictionaries look values up by key.
Comprehensions build lists in one expressive line.

lessons.title: Python mini project: a password strength checker

concept.text: You will write a small tool that scores a password and explains what is weak about it. It combines functions, strings, loops and conditionals, and it is your first taste of security tooling.
concept.analogy: The checker is a bouncer with a checklist: long enough? Has a digit? Has a symbol? Each tick earns a point, and you need enough points to get in.

steps.title: Write the rules
steps.text: `any()` returns True if at least one character passes a test.
steps.code: has_digit = any(c.isdigit() for c in password)

steps.title: Collect feedback
steps.text: Store each rule as a description and a result, then loop over them to build a score and a list of tips.

steps.title: Return a verdict
steps.text: Map the score to a label and print the tips for failed rules.

interactive.starter:
def check(password):
    rules = {
        "at least 12 characters": len(password) >= 12,
        "a lowercase letter": any(c.islower() for c in password),
        "an uppercase letter": any(c.isupper() for c in password),
        "a digit": any(c.isdigit() for c in password),
        "a symbol": any(not c.isalnum() for c in password),
    }
    score = sum(rules.values())
    verdict = "strong" if score == 5 else "ok" if score >= 3 else "weak"
    print(f"{password!r}: {verdict} ({score}/5)")
    for rule, passed in rules.items():
        if not passed:
            print("  - add", rule)

check("password")
check("Tr0ub4dor&3")
check("correct-Horse-battery-9")

challenge.prompt: Add a sixth rule: the password must not be in a list of common passwords (`password`, `123456`, `qwerty`, `letmein`). A common password should always be rated weak, whatever its score.
challenge.hint: Create `COMMON = {"password", ...}` and check `password.lower() in COMMON` before computing the verdict.

takeaways: A dictionary of rule name to result makes checks easy to add and report on.
any() and generator expressions test characters without manual loops.
Real tools are small pieces of logic composed together.
